query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Inducing a controlled degree of Cu segregation in the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating will promote the formation of a nanocrystalline, Cu‐rich surface glaze during high-temperature sliding, which in turn shifts the microscopic deformation from localized shear to more homogeneous plastic flow and lowers the overall wear rate.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating on a conventional metal substrate with a relatively uniform, solid-solution microstructure.
generation.intervention: A post-deposition heat treatment process designed to promote moderate Cu segregation at grain boundaries without excessive coarsening.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests performed in the high-temperature regime (e.g., 500–700 °C) where diffusion and dynamic recrystallization are active—ideally under an inert or controlled atmosphere to minimize oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Cu‐rich nano-precipitates at grain boundaries and the resulting ultra-nanocrystalline dynamic surface glaze layer induced during sliding.
generation.mechanism: The controlled heat treatment partially segregates Cu, which reduces local lattice cohesion and acts to pin dislocations. Under high-temperature sliding, this leads to dynamic recrystallization and formation of a fine-grained (nanocrystalline) surface layer. This layer distributes deformation more uniformly, suppressing localized shear and crack initiation, thereby reducing wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-deposited baseline, the heat-treated coating will exhibit a lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate, with microstructural analysis showing a finer, Cu-rich nanocrystalline surface layer and a shift from localized to more homogeneous plastic deformation during sliding.
generation.baseline: The untreated (as-deposited) FeNiCrCoCu coating lacking promoted Cu segregation and with a coarser, uniform solid-solution microstructure.
generation.boundary: The predictions are expected to hold under high-temperature sliding conditions where sufficient thermal activation allows for dynamic grain refinement. Excessive heat treatment leading to over-segregation or grain coarsening, or operating conditions with severe oxidative environments, may deviate from the expected behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal heat treatment parameters (temperature, time) needed to achieve beneficial Cu segregation without detrimental coarsening are uncertain, as is the precise quantitative reduction in wear rate.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on identical metal substrates. Subject one set to the proposed post-deposition heat treatment aimed at inducing controlled Cu segregation, while leaving the other set as-deposited. Conduct sliding wear tests at a controlled high temperature (e.g., 600 °C) under identical loads and sliding speeds in an inert atmosphere. Analyze both the macroscopic wear rates and the microscopic deformation behavior using SEM, TEM, and EDS to assess grain size, Cu segregation, and deformation modes.
measurements: Grain size and Cu segregation (via TEM/EDS)
Deformation mechanism indicators (e.g., dislocation density, presence of nanocrystalline glaze layer)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated coatings do not show a statistically significant decrease in wear rate and friction coefficient, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal the expected Cu-rich nanocrystalline surface layer and corresponding shift in deformation mechanism relative to the as-deposited coatings, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
